beats.say: At 3 a.m. your container dies. With Docker alone, it stays dead.
Docker runs what you tell it, once. Nobody watches it for you.
beats.label: Docker alone
beats.head: It runs once. Nobody watches.

beats.say: This port has three ideas: the control loop, the pod, and the manifest.
beats.label: Port 1 · Fundamentals

check.prompt: You ask for three copies and one dies. What does Kubernetes do?
options: Nothing, until you run a command
check.why: A controller compares what you asked for with what exists, and fixes the difference.

beats.say: First: the one idea behind all of Kubernetes.
You declare what you want. For example: three copies of my app.
beats.label: Desired state
beats.head: You say what you want

beats.say: A controller observes, compares, and acts. Then it does that again, without end.
beats.label: The loop

beats.say: It runs pods. A pod is one or more containers that share one address.
beats.label: Pod
beats.head: Containers that share one IP

beats.say: Most pods hold one container. Think of a pod as a wrapper around it.
beats.label: In practice
beats.head: Usually one container per pod

check.prompt: You delete a pod that has no controller. What happens?
check.why: The kubelet restarts a crashed container. Nothing recreates a bare pod that is deleted.

beats.say: If a container crashes, the node restarts it inside the same pod.
beats.label: A crash
beats.head: The node restarts the container

beats.say: But if you delete a bare pod, nothing brings it back. That is why controllers exist.
beats.label: A delete
beats.head: A deleted pod stays gone

beats.say: Last: how do you say what you want?
You write a file. You fill in the spec, and the cluster fills in the status.
beats.label: A manifest
beats.head: You write spec. It writes status.

beats.say: Declare, do not command. A pod wraps containers. And a bare pod does not come back.
beats.label: Fundamentals

beats.say: Now start the first lesson below.
